placeholders.name: DESCRIBE THE TASK IN ONE SENTENCE
placeholders.what: State the actual task you picked from your scored list of five, in a single plain sentence. Don't write a vague label like "clean up notes" — name exactly what needs to happen so the AI (and you, later, when judging the result) know what success means.
examples: Summarize this week's five customer support email threads into one paragraph per customer for my Monday huddle.
Turn my rough handwritten notes from today's supplier call into a clean recap email.
Draft a first-pass reply to this vendor's contract renewal email.

placeholders.name: PASTE OR DESCRIBE THE INPUT — e.g., an email thread, notes, a data export
placeholders.what: The real material the AI needs to do the task — paste the actual text whenever you can, rather than describing it in your own words. A description forces the AI to guess at details a direct paste would have given it for free.
examples:
Thread 1 (Jane R.): "My order #4482 arrived with the wrong size, size M instead of L." Reply: "So sorry! Sending correct size overnight, no charge, keep the M." Jane: "Thank you, that's great service."
Thread 2 (Tom K.): "Still no shipping confirmation after 6 days." Reply: "Checking with warehouse now." No further reply from Tom yet.

Notes from call w/ Riverside Supply 8/9: they're raising unit price 6% starting Oct 1, said it's due to freight costs, offered to lock current price if we commit to 12-month contract, need answer by 8/20
Vendor email: "Your annual contract renews Sept 1 at $4,200/year, a 3% increase from last year. Let us know by Aug 15 if you'd like to discuss terms."

placeholders.name: e.g., "a 200-word email", "a bulleted list", "a short table"
placeholders.what: The exact shape the output needs to take, based on where it's going next (a Slack message, an email, a doc you'll paste into a meeting). Naming this precisely avoids the most common source of wasted rework: a good draft in the wrong format.
examples: A 150-word email ready to send
A bulleted list, one bullet per customer, under 40 words each
A short table with three columns: Customer, Issue, Status

placeholders.name: e.g., "matches our usual tone", "covers all three items", "flags anything ambiguous instead of guessing"
placeholders.what: One sentence describing what a genuinely good result looks like, written before you see any draft. This gives you a fixed standard to check the output against, instead of judging it against a feeling you never wrote down.
examples: Sounds like something I'd actually say out loud to a customer, not corporate-sounding
Covers all five customer threads with nothing left out
Flags any thread where the resolution status isn't clear instead of guessing it was resolved

placeholders.name: DESCRIBE — e.g., direct and friendly, formal, concise
placeholders.what: The tone you want, matched to who's actually reading this. Naming it explicitly stops the AI from defaulting to a generic, overly formal register.
examples: Direct and friendly — for regular customers
Formal and precise — for a legal or compliance-sensitive message
Warm but brief — for a quick update to a longtime client

variations.label: Quick version for a small daily task
variations.whenToUse: Use this for genuinely low-stakes, low-risk items — formatting notes, drafting a routine internal message — where the full brief ceremony is overkill and would slow you down more than it helps.
variations.prompt:
Do this task for me: [DESCRIBE THE TASK IN ONE SENTENCE]

Here's what you need:
[PASTE THE SOURCE MATERIAL]

Give it to me as [FORMAT]. Use only what's in the source material — don't invent anything. If something's missing, just note it briefly at the end instead of guessing.

variations.label: When you're stuck picking which task to delegate first
variations.whenToUse: Use this before the delegation prompt itself, if you have a list of candidate tasks but aren't sure which one scores best on clarity, speed to check, and time saved.
variations.prompt:
I'm choosing my first task to delegate to AI. Here are five candidates from my past week:
[LIST YOUR FIVE TASKS, ONE LINE EACH]

For each one, score it 1-5 on: (1) how clear the 'right answer' is, (2) how fast I could check the output against a source, (3) how much real time it costs me to do it myself. Then recommend which one I should delegate first, and explain why in two sentences — favor a task that's easy to verify over one that just seems important.

variations.label: Recurring version — turn it into a reusable template
variations.whenToUse: Use this once your first delegation of a task type worked well and you know you'll repeat it weekly or monthly — it saves you from rewriting the brief from scratch every time.
variations.prompt:
Based on this successful brief and result, help me turn it into a reusable template I can fill in fast next time.

Original brief and source: [PASTE YOUR ORIGINAL BRIEF]
What worked well about the result: [NOTE WHAT WAS GOOD]
What I had to fix by hand: [NOTE ANY EDITS YOU MADE]

Give me a fill-in-the-blank version of this brief with clear bracketed fields, so next time I only need to swap in new source material and a couple of details.

followUps.label: Check nothing was invented
followUps.prompt: Before I use this, go back through your draft line by line and confirm every fact, name, date, and number traces directly back to my source material. List anything that doesn't, or anything you inferred rather than found stated directly.

followUps.label: Wrong format? Reshape it
followUps.prompt: This is close, but reformat it as [the format you actually need] — keep the same content and facts, just restructure how it's presented.

followUps.label: Sounds too generic or robotic
followUps.prompt: This reads too generic. Rewrite it in a more [direct / casual / formal] tone — like I'd actually say it out loud, not like a template anyone could have written.

followUps.label: Cut it down
followUps.prompt: Cut this down by about half without losing any of the required facts. Tighten the wording — don't just delete sentences and leave gaps.

biz-b1-delegate-first-task.walkthrough:
Dana runs a five-person landscaping supply business and wants to try delegating something small before trusting AI with anything bigger.

She lists five tasks from the past week: writing a supplier follow-up email, summarizing customer support threads for Monday's team meeting, drafting a job posting, reconciling a spreadsheet, and writing a thank-you note to a longtime client. She scores each on how clear the right answer is, how fast she can check it, and how much time it actually costs her — the support-thread summary wins, because she can check it in about two minutes against the real emails.

She opens Claude, pastes the delegation prompt, and fills in the brackets: TASK becomes "Summarize this week's five customer support email threads into one bullet per customer for Monday's huddle." SOURCE MATERIAL is the actual five email threads, copied straight out of her inbox. FORMAT is "a bulleted list, one bullet per customer, under 40 words each." DONE WELL is "covers the issue, the resolution status, and whether the customer seems at risk of leaving." TONE is "direct, the way I'd say it in the meeting."

Claude returns five bullets. Four are solid and clearly grounded in the emails. The fifth flags a genuine gap: one thread never actually confirmed whether a refund was processed, so instead of guessing, Claude lists it under "Questions before I finalize this" rather than stating it as resolved.

Dana sends the follow-up "Check nothing was invented." Claude re-confirms the four solid bullets and leaves the flagged question exactly as it was. Dana checks the real email thread herself, finds the answer was buried in a later message, and adds one line by hand.

Total time: about twelve minutes, against the twenty-five minutes this summary usually eats out of her Sunday night.

placeholders.name: announcement / routine reply / difficult message — describe: complaint, mistake, price change, delay, etc.
placeholders.what: Which of the three message types this is, and if it's a difficult message, the specific kind. This one choice reshapes the whole structure of the draft — a price-change announcement and a complaint reply need very different openings.
examples: Difficult message — a shipping delay, replying to a customer who already emailed twice asking where their order is
Announcement — a price increase taking effect next month for all subscribers
Routine reply — a customer asking about our return policy

placeholders.name: e.g., all customers, one specific customer, a customer who left a negative review
placeholders.what: Who actually receives this message — determines whether the draft is personalized to one person's situation or written to work for a broad list of recipients.
examples: One specific customer — the one who emailed twice this week about a late order
All active subscribers on our email list
A customer who left a 2-star Google review mentioning slow service

placeholders.name: email, SMS, review reply, social post
placeholders.what: The channel this message goes out on, which changes the expected length and formality.
examples: Email
Public review reply (Google/Yelp)
SMS — must fit in 2-3 short sentences

placeholders.name: WHAT HAPPENED
placeholders.what: The plain facts of the situation, stated neutrally — not a spun version, just what actually occurred.
examples: Our fulfillment partner had a system outage that delayed all orders placed May 3-5 by about 4 days.
A customer received the wrong item size in their order.
We're raising our monthly subscription price from $29 to $34 starting next billing cycle.

placeholders.name: WHAT WE'RE DOING ABOUT IT
placeholders.what: Your actual response or fix, described plainly — the concrete action already underway or decided, not a vague promise.
examples: We're proactively emailing every affected customer with an updated delivery estimate.
We're shipping the correct size overnight at no charge and providing a prepaid label to return the wrong item.
Nothing needed from the customer — the new price applies automatically at their next renewal.

placeholders.name: WHAT I CAN ACTUALLY OFFER OR COMMIT TO, IF ANYTHING
placeholders.what: A real, already-decided offer — a discount, a refund, or genuinely nothing. This is the single most important field in the whole prompt: never leave it blank and let the AI improvise something you'll have to honor.
examples: A 10% discount code on their next order
A full refund of shipping costs for this order
Nothing beyond the fix already described — no discount is being offered

placeholders.name: e.g., warm and direct, formal and brief, apologetic without being defensive
placeholders.what: The tone that fits both the situation and the channel — an apology and a routine reply should not sound the same.
examples: Apologetic without being defensive — for a mistake we caused
Warm and direct — for a routine policy reply
Formal and brief — for a price-increase announcement to all customers

placeholders.name: LENGTH
placeholders.what: The target length, matched to the channel — a review reply and an email have very different reasonable lengths.
examples: Under 120 words
3-4 sentences
Under 300 characters, for SMS

variations.label: Quick version for a routine one-line reply
variations.whenToUse: Use this for simple, low-stakes replies — a policy question, a shipping-status check-in — where the full facts-and-tone structure is more ceremony than the situation needs.
variations.prompt:
Write a quick, [TONE] reply to this customer message: [PASTE THEIR MESSAGE]

Here's the actual answer: [YOUR ANSWER/FACTS]

Keep it under [LENGTH]. Don't add a commitment, discount, or explanation beyond what I've given you.

variations.label: Public review reply version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when responding to a negative public review, where the real audience is both the reviewer and everyone else who will read the reply later.
variations.prompt:
Help me reply to this public review. Remember other potential customers will read this reply too, not just the reviewer.

THE REVIEW: [PASTE THE REVIEW TEXT]
WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED (our side, factually): [FACTS]
WHAT WE'RE DOING ABOUT IT: [FIX OR RESPONSE]
WHAT I CAN OFFER, IF ANYTHING: [OFFER OR "NOTHING"]

Write a short, professional public reply under [LENGTH] that acknowledges the experience without being defensive, states our side factually without arguing, and shows future readers we take feedback seriously — without generic phrases like "we take this very seriously."

variations.label: Multi-channel announcement version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the same announcement needs to go out as both a longer email and a shorter social post, so the core facts stay consistent across both.
variations.prompt:
Help me write the same announcement in two formats using these facts.

FACTS (use only these): [WHAT HAPPENED] / [WHAT WE'RE DOING ABOUT IT] / [WHAT I CAN OFFER, IF ANYTHING]
TONE: [TONE]

1. An email version, under [LENGTH], with a clear subject line.
2. A social post version, under 280 characters, same core facts, no invented details.

Both versions must state the exact same facts — don't add anything to one version that isn't in the other.

followUps.label: Check for overcommitment
followUps.prompt: Go back through this draft and highlight anything it states as a commitment — a discount, a timeline, an exception — that I didn't explicitly give you in the facts. I want to catch anything invented before I send this.

followUps.label: Too defensive or over-apologetic
followUps.prompt: Read this back for tone. Does it sound defensive, or apologize more than the situation calls for? Rewrite it to state the situation plainly once and move to the resolution, without over-apologizing.

followUps.label: Needs to be shorter for SMS or social
followUps.prompt: Cut this down to under [target length/character count] while keeping the core fact, the fix, and the offer (if any) intact. Drop anything else first.

followUps.label: Add my own opening line
followUps.prompt: Leave the body as is, but suggest two different personalized opening lines I could hand-write myself to replace the generic opener — one warmer, one more brief and direct.

biz-b2-customer-communication.walkthrough:
Marcus owns a small online kitchenware store. A fulfillment partner's system outage delayed every order placed between May 3rd and 5th by about four days, and one customer, Priya, has already emailed twice asking where her order is.

Before opening any AI tool, Marcus writes down the three facts in plain language: what happened (the outage delayed shipments by about four days), what he's doing about it (proactively emailing every affected customer with a new estimate), and what he can actually offer (a 10% discount code on their next order — he already cleared this with his bookkeeper). He identifies this as a difficult message: a delay complaint, one-to-one, to a customer who already emailed twice.

He pastes the customer-message prompt into Claude and fills in: MESSAGE TYPE — difficult message, delay, replying to someone who's already followed up twice; AUDIENCE — Priya specifically; CHANNEL — email; the three FACTS fields with his exact notes; TONE — apologetic without being defensive; LENGTH — under 120 words.

The draft opens by acknowledging the delay and her frustration directly, states the outage reason in one sentence without over-explaining, gives the new expected delivery window, and offers the discount as a bracketed [DISCOUNT CODE] placeholder rather than inventing a percentage.

Marcus reads it and it's close, but the second sentence still feels a little stiff. He sends the follow-up "Too defensive or over-apologetic," and the rewrite trims one apologetic phrase and gets more direct. He swaps in his real discount code, adds Priya's name to the opening by hand, and sends it.

Total time: about eight minutes, and Priya replies within the hour thanking him for the update.

placeholders.name: MARKET/INDUSTRY, with region and customer segment — e.g., "small-business bookkeeping services for companies under 20 employees in [CITY/REGION]"
placeholders.what: A precise description of your market — industry, region, and the type of customer you serve — not just an industry label. This is the single biggest lever on whether the research comes back useful or so broad it's meaningless.
examples: Boutique fitness studios (yoga/pilates) serving adults 25-45 in Portland, Oregon
Freelance graphic design services for early-stage SaaS startups, US-based clients
Residential HVAC repair and maintenance for homeowners in the Dallas-Fort Worth metro area

placeholders.name: YOUR DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE
placeholders.what: The actual decision this research needs to support — not the general topic you're curious about, but the specific call you're about to make.
examples: Whether to raise my web-design retainer from $1,800 to $2,200/month
Whether to open a second studio location in the suburbs
Whether to add a rush-service tier and what to charge for it

placeholders.name: NAMED COMPETITORS, if any
placeholders.what: Two or three specific competitors you already know of, by name, so Gemini grounds its answer in your actual competitive set instead of a generic industry overview.
examples: Riverside Fitness Co. and Sunrise Yoga Studio
None known yet — please identify 3 likely competitors in this niche and segment
BrightPath Design Co. and Halo Creative

variations.label: Quick single-question gut-check
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you just need one fast data point — for example, before a call today — rather than the full four-part research brief.
variations.prompt: Quick check, with cited sources: what are typical prices right now for [SERVICE/PRODUCT] among businesses like [NAMED COMPETITORS OR MARKET DESCRIPTION]? Cite the source and date for each figure, and flag if you had to widen beyond my specific market to find an answer.

variations.label: When you don't have any named competitors yet
variations.whenToUse: Use this first, before the main research prompt, if you're scoping a market you don't know well and can't yet name specific competitors.
variations.prompt: I'm researching [MARKET/INDUSTRY, WITH REGION AND SEGMENT]. I don't have specific competitor names yet. Identify 3-5 businesses that would realistically compete with a business like mine in this exact niche and region, with a cited source for each (their website, a directory listing, a review site). Once I have this list, I'll use it to run deeper pricing and positioning research.

variations.label: Pricing-only deep dive
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the decision is specifically about pricing (a rate increase, a new tier) and you want more numeric depth than the general four-part research prompt gives you.
variations.prompt:
I'm deciding: [YOUR PRICING DECISION IN ONE SENTENCE]. Research current pricing specifically, with a cited source and date for each figure:
1. What do [NAMED COMPETITORS] charge for the closest comparable offering, broken down by tier if they have one?
2. What's the actual price range across this market segment, low to high, not just an average?
3. Has pricing in this market moved in the last 12 months, and in which direction?
4. What would a customer likely perceive as the 'expected' price point before they even ask?

Flag any figure you're not confident in rather than stating it with false precision.

followUps.label: Open and verify the sources
followUps.prompt: For the top 3 most important figures in your answer, give me the direct link to the source and the exact sentence in that source the figure came from, so I can verify it myself.

followUps.label: Narrow to my exact situation
followUps.prompt: That's broader than I need. Narrow this specifically to businesses at my scale and price point — [YOUR SCALE/PRICE POINT] — and tell me if the answer changes when you exclude larger or much smaller players.

followUps.label: Turn it into a decision memo
followUps.prompt: Compile everything above into a short decision memo I could show a co-founder or lender: the decision, the 3-4 key findings with sources, and a one-line recommendation. Keep the source links visible.

followUps.label: Argue the other side
followUps.prompt: Now argue against the decision I'm leaning toward, using only what this research actually shows. What's the strongest case for NOT doing this, based on the data you found?

biz-i1-market-competitor-research-perple.walkthrough:
Priya runs a solo web design business and is weighing whether to raise her retainer from $1,800 to $2,200 a month, but she hasn't checked what comparable designers actually charge in over a year.

She opens the Gemini app and selects Deep Research. For the decision, she states it in one sentence: "Whether to raise my web-design retainer from $1,800 to $2,200/month." For the market field, she writes "freelance web design retainers for small B2B service businesses, US-based clients." She doesn't have specific named competitors, so she leaves that field noting she isn't sure of exact competitors at her scale.

She pastes the full research prompt, asking for cited, dated sources on what comparable providers charge, whether the broader market has moved recently, any notable shifts, and what a prospective client would compare her offer against — with a flag if Gemini had to widen beyond her segment to find data. Deep Research shows her a short research plan before running; she skims it, confirms it's searching recent freelance-pricing sources, and lets it proceed.

The answer comes back citing four sources: two freelancer rate surveys from the past year, a pricing page from a small studio, and a blog post on agency pricing trends. It notes that retainers in her segment commonly run $1,800-$2,600 depending on scope, that rates have trended up roughly 8-10% over the past year due to demand, and flags that one figure came from a broader freelance-market survey not specific to web design.

Priya sends the follow-up "Open and verify the sources" and personally checks two of the four links — both hold up. She then asks it to compile a short decision memo. With the cited range in hand, she decides $2,200 is reasonable and not out of step with the market.

Total time: about eighteen minutes, including opening the source links herself.

placeholders.name: PASTE OR DESCRIBE THE TASK STEP BY STEP, AS MESSY AS IT ACTUALLY IS
placeholders.what: Your real, unfiltered walkthrough of how you actually do this task — written or dictated like you're explaining it to a new hire standing next to you, including the exceptions and judgment calls, not a cleaned-up idealized version.
examples: When a new client signs, I check if they came from referral or the website form — referrals skip the qualification call. I send the welcome email, but if it's a rush project I call first same day. I add them to the project tracker and tag by service type. If they haven't sent a deposit within 3 days I follow up once, then loop in my business partner if still nothing after a week.

Every Friday I pull the week's sales numbers from the POS system into a spreadsheet. If a category is down more than 10% from last week I flag it in yellow. I email the summary to the owner by end of day, unless it's a holiday week, in which case I send it Monday instead.

When a refund request comes in, I check the order date first — anything past 30 days gets a store credit instead of a cash refund unless the item arrived damaged, which always gets a full cash refund regardless of date. I process it in the system, then send a confirmation email.

placeholders.name: N
placeholders.what: This isn't something you type into the prompt — it's a token that appears inside the AI's generated SOP output, not something you fill in beforehand. [N] marks a step number the AI references inside a decision-point instruction, like "do Y instead of continuing to step 4." You don't need to do anything with it beyond understanding what it means when you read the finished SOP.
examples: "If the client already paid, skip ahead to step 6."
"If the item arrived damaged, process the full refund instead of continuing to step 3."
"If it's a rush order, call the client immediately instead of continuing to step 2."

placeholders.name: NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...
placeholders.what: Also not something you fill in — it's a tag the AI uses inside its own generated SOP to flag a real gap in your walkthrough, instead of guessing at a step you never actually described. When this tag shows up in the output, it's telling you to go back and either explain that part yourself or fill it in by hand.
examples: "[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: What happens if the customer never responds to the follow-up after one week?]"
"[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: Who approves the refund if it's over $200?]"
"[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: What tag should be used if the client doesn't fit clearly into one service category?]"

variations.label: Quick version for a short, simple task
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a task with only a handful of steps and no real decision points, where the full six-section SOP structure would be overkill.
variations.prompt:
Turn this short process into a simple numbered checklist, not a full SOP:

[PASTE THE TASK, AS MESSY AS IT ACTUALLY IS]

Just give me: numbered steps, and a one-line note on what 'done' looks like. Use only what I described — don't add steps I didn't mention.

variations.label: When you're documenting a teammate's process, not your own
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you're interviewing someone else on your team about how they do a task, rather than writing up your own process.
variations.prompt:
I interviewed a team member about how they do a task and I'm going to paste their raw explanation below, in their own words (not mine). Turn this into a clear SOP using the same structure as before.

Team member's raw walkthrough: [PASTE THEIR DESCRIPTION]

Use the same 6-section structure: purpose, when to use/not use, numbered steps, decision points, common mistakes, and what 'done' looks like. If anything in their explanation is ambiguous or contradicts itself, flag it as "[NEEDS CLARIFICATION: ...]" rather than guessing what they meant — I'll follow up with them directly.

variations.label: Decision-tree-first version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for a task with several branching decision points, where a visual-style decision summary at the top would help someone scan faster than reading every numbered step.
variations.prompt:
Turn this raw walkthrough into an SOP, but lead with a short decision-tree summary before the full steps.

My raw walkthrough: [PASTE OR DESCRIBE THE TASK STEP BY STEP, AS MESSY AS IT ACTUALLY IS]

First, give me a short 'decision tree at a glance' section: each decision point as a simple if/then line, in the order someone would hit them. Then give me the full 6-section SOP as before. Use only what I described.

followUps.label: Fold in gaps found during the real test
followUps.prompt: I had a teammate test this SOP and they got stuck at [DESCRIBE WHERE THEY HESITATED OR ASKED A QUESTION]. Revise that section to close the gap, based only on how I actually handle that situation: [YOUR ANSWER].

followUps.label: Shorten it to a one-page quick reference
followUps.prompt: Condense this into a one-page quick-reference version — just the numbered steps and decision points, no purpose/mistakes sections — for someone who's already read the full SOP once and just needs a refresher.

followUps.label: Strengthen the common-mistakes section
followUps.prompt: Expand the common mistakes section with 2-3 more specific mistakes people are likely to make on this exact task, based only on the decision points and exceptions I described — not generic advice.

followUps.label: Double-check nothing was added
followUps.prompt: Go back through the SOP and list any step, tool, or best practice that isn't something I explicitly described in my raw walkthrough. I want to catch anything you added before I hand this to my team.

biz-i2-standard-operating-procedures.walkthrough:
Renata runs a small marketing agency and wants to hand off new-client onboarding to her office manager, but she's never written down exactly how she does it.

She opens Claude and, instead of trying to write something tidy, types out her real process as messily as it actually happens: how she checks whether a client came from a referral or the website form (referrals skip the qualification call), how she sends the welcome email but calls first same-day if it's a rush project, how she tags them in the project tracker, and the exact sequence for chasing an unpaid deposit — one follow-up after 3 days, then looping in her business partner after a week if there's still nothing.

She pastes this into the SOP prompt exactly as written, typos and all, as the raw walkthrough. Claude returns a structured document: a one-sentence purpose, a "when to use / when not to" section noting this only applies to new signed clients (not renewals), numbered steps with the referral-vs-form decision clearly marked as its own branch, the rush-project exception called out explicitly rather than buried in a paragraph, and the 3-day/1-week follow-up sequence as its own numbered mini-process.

Renata reads it against what she actually does — it matches. She hands it to her office manager, Beth, and watches her attempt the next real client signup using only the document. Beth hesitates at one point: the SOP doesn't say what tag to use for a client who doesn't clearly fit one service category.

Renata sends the follow-up "Fold in gaps found during the real test," describing what she actually does in that situation, and the SOP gets a one-line fix. She saves the final version in the shared drive with a six-month review reminder.

Total time: about twenty minutes, plus the real test run with Beth the following week.

placeholders.name: PASTE YOUR TABLE — e.g., line items with this period vs. last period, or vs. same period last year
placeholders.what: Your actual figures, pasted as a simple table or list — line items with this period's number next to the comparison period's number. Redact customer names or account details you don't need for the narrative before pasting.
examples:
Revenue: $84,200 (this quarter) vs. $76,500 (last quarter)
COGS: 43% of revenue (this quarter) vs. 38% (last quarter)
Marketing spend: $6,100 (this quarter) vs. $6,000 (last quarter)
Net profit margin: 11% (this quarter) vs. 15% (last quarter)

March revenue: $22,400 vs. February: $18,900
March new customers: 31 vs. February: 19
March refunds: $1,800 vs. February: $600

Payroll: $41,000 (Q2) vs. $38,500 (Q1)
Rent: $6,000 flat both quarters
Software/subscriptions: $2,300 (Q2) vs. $1,900 (Q1)

placeholders.name: E.G., "WE RAN A PROMOTION IN MARCH" OR LEAVE BLANK
placeholders.what: Any real, known reason behind a number change that you can state with confidence — optional, and only include something you actually know happened, never a guess dressed up as fact.
examples: We ran a 20%-off promotion for the first two weeks of March
Our biggest client paused their contract in April
(leave blank — I don't have additional context to add)

variations.label: Quick version for one specific number
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you only need to explain a single line item — for example, right before a meeting where you know someone will ask about one specific number — rather than a full narrative.
variations.prompt:
I need to explain one number change in plain English. Here's the data: [THIS PERIOD'S FIGURE] vs. [LAST PERIOD'S FIGURE] for [LINE ITEM].

Describe the size and direction of the change in one or two sentences a non-finance person could follow. Do not invent a reason for the change unless I tell you one: [KNOWN REASON, OR LEAVE BLANK]. If you can't explain it from the numbers alone, say so directly.

variations.label: Multi-period trend version
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you have three or more periods of data and want to see the trend line, not just a single period-over-period comparison.
variations.prompt:
I'm going to give you the same line items across several periods. Write a plain-English trend narrative, not just a single comparison.

Figures across periods:
[PASTE YOUR TABLE, WITH ONE COLUMN PER PERIOD]

RULES: Only describe what the numbers show. Do not invent a business reason for a trend unless I've told you one below. Known context: [OPTIONAL CONTEXT OR LEAVE BLANK]

Structure: 1) overall trend summary, 2) the line item with the most consistent movement across periods, 3) any period that breaks the trend and is worth a closer look, 4) changes I can't explain from the numbers alone, 5) three questions for my bookkeeper or accountant.

variations.label: For a specific external audience

biz-i3-financial-narratives.walkthrough:
Oskar owns a small specialty coffee roasting business and has a call with his business partner tomorrow where he knows he'll be asked why margin dropped this quarter, and he doesn't have a confident answer yet.

He pulls his quarterly P&L export and redacts anything beyond the aggregate line items. He opens ChatGPT and pastes the financial-narrative prompt, filling in the figures table: revenue $84,200 this quarter versus $76,500 last quarter, cost of goods sold at 43% of revenue versus 38%, and marketing spend essentially flat. He leaves the known-context field blank because he genuinely doesn't know why COGS moved.

The response opens with a one-paragraph summary: revenue grew about 10%, but gross margin compressed roughly 5 points, driven by the jump in COGS as a share of revenue. It states this plainly as fact, backed by the actual figures. Under "changes I can't explain from the numbers alone," it flags the COGS increase directly and doesn't guess at a cause. It closes with three questions for his bookkeeper: did a supplier raise prices, did product mix shift toward higher-cost items, or was there a one-off inventory write-off this quarter.

Oskar reads it and sends the follow-up "Turn it into talking points," since he wants to say this out loud tomorrow rather than read from a document. He gets five short, plain-language points back, practices them once, and emails his bookkeeper the three questions before the call.

By the time he's on the call, he can state the revenue growth and margin compression confidently, and honestly says the cause is still being confirmed rather than guessing at one.

Total time: about fifteen minutes.

fl-b1-proposals-that-win.walkthrough:
Tanya is a freelance copywriter who just found a job post from a seed-stage SaaS company asking for a landing page rewrite, and she wants to send a proposal today before the post gets buried.

fl-i1-scope-quote-contract-drafts.walkthrough:
Ingrid is a freelance brand designer who just had a call with a new client, a coffee roastery, about a four-week brand identity project, and needs to send a scope, quote, and contract before the client commits to another designer.

She opens Claude and pastes the scope/quote/contract prompt. PROJECT BRIEF: "a brand identity project for a new boutique coffee roastery, including logo, color palette, and brand guidelines." DELIVERABLES: "logo files (vector + PNG), a one-page brand guideline PDF, and 3 rounds of revisions." REVISIONS INCLUDED: "2." TIMELINE: "4 weeks from signed contract and deposit received." EXCLUSIONS: "does not include website implementation, printed materials, or packaging design." PAYMENT TERMS: "50% deposit before work begins, remaining 50% due on delivery, net 15." PRICING STRUCTURE: "flat project fee of $3,200."

The draft comes back with a plain-language scope stating exactly what's included and explicitly what's excluded, a quote broken into line items — logo design, brand guidelines, and revisions, not one lump total — and standard payment clauses matching her 50%/net-15 structure exactly. It also produces a clearly separated section titled "Have a professional review before signing," covering IP/ownership transfer, liability limitation, and termination terms, with starting language drafted but explicitly marked as needing review.

Ingrid notices the deliverables list says "3 rounds of revisions" while she'd said 2 in the revisions field — a small inconsistency from typing it into the wrong field. She sends the follow-up "Check payment terms match exactly" style correction directly, restating "2 rounds of revisions," and it's fixed.

She sends the scope and quote to the client for written approval first, and only after they confirm, sends the flagged clauses to a lawyer for a quick review before the contract goes out for signature.

Total time: about twenty minutes drafting, plus a short paid lawyer review before signing.

placeholders.name: WHAT THEY NEEDED / THE PROBLEM
placeholders.what: The client's actual situation or problem before you started — stated plainly, the way you'd explain it to another freelancer.
examples: A small e-commerce client's checkout completion rate was low and they suspected slow page load times were the cause.
A local bakery had no consistent brand identity across their packaging, signage, and Instagram.
A startup's onboarding emails had a high unsubscribe rate in the first week after signup.

placeholders.name: YOUR ACTUAL WORK
placeholders.what: What you specifically did — real actions you took, not a vague description like "improved their website."
examples: Optimized product images for faster load times and simplified the checkout flow from 4 steps to 2.
Designed a cohesive brand identity — logo, color palette, and packaging templates — and applied it across their Instagram and physical packaging.
Rewrote the 5-email onboarding sequence to lead with a single clear next action instead of multiple competing calls-to-action.

placeholders.name: REAL OUTCOME — A NUMBER, A SPECIFIC CHANGE, A QUOTE — OR STATE IF THERE'S NO HARD METRIC
placeholders.what: The genuine result, exactly as you know it — a real number if you have one, a specific observed change if you don't, or an honest statement that there's no hard metric to cite.
examples: Checkout completion rate went up; the client reported roughly 15% more completed orders over the following month, per their own analytics.
No hard metric available, but the client said their packaging finally 'looks like a real brand' and re-ordered the same packaging design for a second product line.
Unsubscribe rate in the first week dropped from about 8% to 3%, based on their email platform's reporting.

placeholders.name: TARGET CLIENT TYPE/INDUSTRY
placeholders.what: The specific type of client you want more of right now — narrow enough that the outreach message can speak directly to their situation.
examples: Small e-commerce businesses with under $2M in annual revenue
Local food and beverage brands preparing to launch a new product line
Early-stage B2B SaaS companies with under 10,000 monthly signups

placeholders.name: SPECIFIC REASON FOR REACHING OUT TO THIS PERSON
placeholders.what: Left blank in the outreach message on purpose — the prompt tells the AI to leave this as a placeholder so you personalize it by hand afterward. A generic-sounding cold message is the biggest tell it wasn't tailored, so this line should reference something real and specific about the person or company you're contacting.
examples: I saw your team just launched a new product page and noticed the checkout flow could use the same treatment I did for [past client]
Came across your recent LinkedIn post about scaling customer onboarding — that's exactly the kind of problem I helped [past client] solve
Noticed you're hiring for a marketing role, which usually means content/design bandwidth is stretched thin — thought this might be useful timing

variations.label: Quick version for a project with no hard metric
variations.whenToUse: Use this when the real result is qualitative — a relationship win, a client quote, a repeat engagement — rather than a number, so the case study leans honestly into that instead of forcing a metric.
variations.prompt:
Help me write a short case study and outreach message for a project with no hard metric to cite.

CLIENT SITUATION: [WHAT THEY NEEDED]
WHAT I DID: [YOUR ACTUAL WORK]
QUALITATIVE OUTCOME (no number available): [DESCRIBE HONESTLY — e.g., a client quote, a repeat engagement, a specific observed change]

Write a 150-200 word case study built around the qualitative outcome, described honestly and specifically — do not invent a number to make it sound more impressive. Then write a short outreach message (under 100 words) for [TARGET CLIENT TYPE], referencing the qualitative result, ending with a low-pressure next step.

variations.label: Batch version — build multiple case studies at once
variations.whenToUse: Use this when you have several past projects and want to build a small set of case studies for different types of results in one pass, rather than one at a time.
variations.prompt:
Help me write short case studies for multiple past projects at once, each using only the real facts given — no invented metrics.

Project 1: Situation: [...] What I did: [...] Result: [...]
Project 2: Situation: [...] What I did: [...] Result: [...]
Project 3: Situation: [...] What I did: [...] Result: [...]

For each, write a 150-200 word case study (situation, approach, result). If a project has no hard metric, describe the qualitative outcome honestly rather than inventing one. Label each case study by the type of result it demonstrates (e.g. 'growth metric,' 'efficiency win,' 'relationship win') so I can pick the most relevant one per pitch.

variations.label: LinkedIn outreach version
variations.whenToUse: Use this for outreach on LinkedIn specifically, where norms and length expectations differ from a cold email.
variations.prompt:
Using this case study, write a short LinkedIn connection request note and a longer follow-up message, aimed at [TARGET CLIENT TYPE/INDUSTRY].

Case study: [PASTE YOUR CASE STUDY]

1. A connection request note under 300 characters, referencing something specific and low-pressure — not a pitch.
2. A follow-up message (to send after they accept) under 100 words, referencing the case study's relevant result and ending with a low-pressure next step. Leave [SPECIFIC REASON FOR REACHING OUT TO THIS PERSON] as a placeholder for me to fill in by hand.

followUps.label: Check no metric was rounded up or invented

followUps.label: Give me alternate opening lines

followUps.prompt: Write a short, low-pressure follow-up message I could send if this person doesn't reply within a week — under 50 words, not pushy, adding one small new piece of value or information rather than just 'checking in.'

fl-i2-marketing-yourself-portfolio-outre.walkthrough:
Devon is a freelance web developer who wants to land more e-commerce clients but hasn't written up any of his past work in a way he could actually send to a prospect.

He picks one real project: a small e-commerce client whose checkout completion rate was low, suspected to be tied to slow page load times. He opens Claude and works through Part 1 of the case-study prompt. CLIENT SITUATION: the slow-load, low-completion problem, stated plainly. WHAT I DID: he optimized product images and simplified checkout from four steps to two. RESULT: checkout completion went up, with the client reporting roughly 15% more completed orders over the following month, based on their own analytics — he's careful to note it's the client's reported figure, not his own independently verified number.

The case study comes back at about 180 words, describing the situation, his specific approach, and the 15% figure attributed clearly to the client's reporting, not stated as an absolute guarantee.

For Part 2, he sets TARGET CLIENT TYPE as "small e-commerce businesses with under $2M in annual revenue," and gets a short outreach message referencing the checkout-completion result specifically, ending with a low-pressure suggestion to share a quick two-minute audit rather than "let's hop on a call."

Devon reads it and it's a touch long for a cold message, so he sends "Tighten the outreach to under 100 words." The revised version keeps the core result and the low-pressure ask, dropping a redundant sentence about his general experience.

He adds his own specific reason for reaching out — he noticed the prospect's site had a similarly slow checkout — and sends it to three prospects that afternoon.

Total time: about sixteen minutes for both the case study and the outreach message.

placeholders.name: routine status update / scope creep pushback / missed deadline / rate increase / other difficult message
placeholders.what: The specific type of message this is — this single choice shapes the whole structure, since a routine update and a rate increase need very different registers.
examples: Scope creep pushback — client asked for two additional pages beyond the agreed scope
Rate increase — first increase in two years for a long-term retainer client
Routine status update — weekly check-in on a project that's on track

placeholders.name: WHAT'S ACTUALLY HAPPENED — PROJECT STATUS, WHAT CHANGED, WHAT WAS ASKED
placeholders.what: The plain facts of the situation, stated neutrally — what the current status is, what changed, or what was requested.
examples: Client asked for two additional landing pages beyond the agreed 3-page scope in the signed contract.
I haven't raised my rate in two years; costs have gone up and my calendar has been consistently full for the last six months.
Design phase is complete and on schedule; development starts Monday as planned.

placeholders.name: WHAT I'M ASKING FOR, OFFERING, OR HOLDING FIRM ON — e.g., "I will do this extra request but it needs a separate quote", "new rate is $X starting [DATE]"
placeholders.what: Your actual, already-decided position — the boundary, ask, or decision you've made before drafting. This is a business call only you should make; never let the draft invent or soften it for you.

New rate is $110/hour, up from $85/hour, starting with projects booked after October 1st.
No ask — this update is for awareness only, nothing needed from the client.

Brief and factual — for a routine status update
Appreciative but clear — for the rate increase, acknowledging the relationship while being direct about the number

placeholders.name: LENGTH
placeholders.what: The target length, matched to how much the situation actually needs said.
examples: Under 100 words
4-5 short paragraphs
2-3 sentences

placeholders.name: EMAIL/MESSAGE PLATFORM

Slack direct message
A comment inside our project management tool (Asana)

fl-i3-client-updates-difficult-conversat.walkthrough:
Amara is a freelance brand strategist who hasn't raised her rate in two years, even though her calendar has been consistently full for the last six months, and she's decided it's time to notify her longest-standing retainer client.

Before opening any AI tool, she decides her actual position first: the new rate is $110/hour, up from $85, effective for projects booked after October 1st. She isn't offering to grandfather in the old rate, and she isn't apologizing for the increase — she's simply informing.

She opens Claude and uses the rate-increase variation of the prompt. MESSAGE TYPE: rate increase. FACTS: she hasn't raised her rate in two years, costs have gone up, and demand for her time has grown steadily. POSITION: new rate is $110/hour starting October 1st. TONE: appreciative but clear. LENGTH: under 100 words.

The first draft states the new rate plainly in the second sentence, includes one genuine line acknowledging their two years of working together, and closes by asking her to confirm she'd like to continue at the new rate for upcoming projects. It's solid, but the closing line reads a little open-ended: "Let me know if you have any questions."

Amara sends the follow-up "Firm up the ask," and the closing becomes more direct: a request to confirm by a specific date whether she wants to continue booking at the new rate, so Amara can plan her calendar accordingly.

She reads the whole thing once more, adds the client's name to the opening by hand, and sends it.

Total time: about nine minutes, and the client replies the next day agreeing to the new rate.

placeholders.name: E.G., "A LANDING PAGE COPY REWRITE", "A BRAND VOICE AUDIT", "AN ONBOARDING EMAIL SEQUENCE"
placeholders.what: The specific type of deliverable you repeat regularly — narrow enough that a standing instruction set can actually be built around it.
examples: A landing page copy rewrite
A brand voice audit
A 5-email onboarding sequence

placeholders.name: DESCRIBE THE SECTIONS, STEPS, OR FORMAT YOU ALWAYS FOLLOW
placeholders.what: Your real, repeatable structure for this deliverable — the sections or steps you follow on essentially every project of this type, described specifically enough that someone else could recognize your work from it.
examples: Hero headline + subhead, three benefit sections, one objection-handling section, one CTA block — always in that order.
Voice audit always covers: current tone assessment, 3 example rewrites in the target voice, a one-page style guide summary, and 5 dos/don'ts.
Sequence is always: welcome + set expectations, quick-win tutorial, social proof, common objection handled, upgrade/next-step nudge.

placeholders.name: E.G., TONE, LENGTH LIMITS, THINGS YOU ALWAYS AVOID
placeholders.what: Your actual quality bar — the specific style rules and things you always avoid, based on real habits you've developed, not generic best practices.
examples: Direct, conversational tone; hero headline always under 10 words; never use the word 'revolutionary' or 'seamless.'
Never write in passive voice; each email under 150 words; always end with exactly one call to action, never two.
Style is warm but not cutesy; avoid exclamation points except in subject lines; always include one concrete number or specific detail per section.

placeholders.name: E.G., CLIENT'S BRAND VOICE SAMPLE, TARGET AUDIENCE, SPECIFIC GOALS
placeholders.what: What genuinely must be custom every time, per client — the inputs you should never assume or fill in generically, because getting them wrong makes the output feel off-brand.
examples: The client's product facts, their target audience description, and a sample of their existing brand voice (an email, a page, anything they've already written).
Their current tone (via 3 example pieces of existing content), their target reader's biggest objection, and their business goals for this quarter.
Their audience's pain points in their own words, any brand words they always/never use, and the specific action they want the reader to take.

followUps.prompt: I ran this workflow on [NUMBER] real projects and it took me [X] hours each time including review. Based on that real time cost and my hourly rate of [RATE], suggest a fixed price for a productized version of this offer.

fl-a1-productize-your-service.walkthrough:
Nadia is a freelance copywriter who has rewritten landing page copy for six different SaaS clients over the past year, and each time she starts from a blank page even though her process barely changes.

She opens Claude and uses the productize prompt. DELIVERABLE TYPE: "a landing page copy rewrite." Her repeatable structure: hero headline plus subhead, three benefit sections, one objection-handling section, one CTA block, always in that order, in a direct conversational tone under a specific word count per section. Her quality bar: never uses the word "revolutionary," headlines always under 10 words. What must be custom every time: the client's actual product facts, their target audience description, and any existing brand voice sample.

The output gives her a standing-instructions block describing that exact five-section structure and her tone rules as the reusable pattern, plus a three-item input checklist — product facts, audience, voice sample — with an explicit instruction to ask rather than assume if any of the three is missing when a new project starts.

She saves this as a Claude Project. Before trusting it on a live client, she runs the follow-up "Test it against a real past project," pasting in the actual inputs from a project she completed two months ago. The output is close to what she actually delivered, but misses that she always writes two headline options, not one — a detail she'd never written down because it was just habit. She adds that line to the instructions.

She then times herself on the next two real client projects: about 40 minutes each including her review pass, down from roughly two hours starting from scratch. Using that real number and her hourly rate, she asks for a price suggestion and sets a $450 fixed price for a "landing page rewrite" package.

Total setup time: about twenty-five minutes, plus the two test runs.
